text: Phantom island, ghost island , sandy island all are correct

In 1970, a twelve-year-old student in Melbourne, Australia, submitted a map of the world as a school assignment. He had drawn his home continent at the top of the page. His teacher marked the project wrong — the map, she said, was upside down.
Nine years later, on Australia Day 1979, Stuart McArthur published his "Universal Corrective Map of the World." Australia sat at the top. Antarctica was below it. The Northern Hemisphere was placed at the bottom of the sheet. The subtitle read with pointed precision: "A corrective for the perpetual Eucentric error of having the South Pole at the bottom." McArthur's argument was geographically unimpeachable: there is no physical reason for north to be "up." The convention had been established by ancient Greek astronomers who lived in the northern hemisphere, formalised by Ptolemy in the 2nd century AD, and perpetuated without serious challenge ever since.
The map sold over 350,000 copies. It is now held in the permanent collections of the British Library and the Library of Congress. McArthur's teacher's name has not been recorded by history.
What is McArthur's map formally called, and what fundamental cartographic assumption — so universal it is almost never examined — does it specifically challenge?
That is the funda, but there’s one specific name for the map
